paras: The lynching of William Steele took place on the night of January 28, 1882, about twelve miles from Logansport, Indiana, when neighbors of a farm woman, Mrs. Buell, pursued and hanged Steele, a man described as a tramp. He was accused of assaulting her after asking for supper, and after the hanging his pursuers piled brush around his body and burned it. A Cincinnati wire dispatch carried the story across the country, often under headlines that called the killing deserved.

According to the wire report, Steele called at Mrs. Buell's farmhouse on a Saturday night and asked her for supper. Finding her alone, the dispatch said, he "outraged her person and fled." Later rewrites added details: the Highland Weekly News said she opened the door and was knocked down, while the Eaton Democrat said the assault took place while she was preparing his meal and that she roused the neighbors after he left. No paper gave Steele's race or any account from him.

The neighbors went after Steele at once; the Highland Weekly News said they "started in all directions" and captured him the same night not far from the house. They hanged him "without delay," by most accounts from a tree. They then piled brush about the body, which the Highland Weekly News said was gathered from the surrounding forest, and burned it "past recognition." No report says how many took part, names any of them, or mentions onlookers.
The sheriff took possession of the body on Monday and turned it over to the coroner. No report of an inquest verdict, arrests or a grand jury inquiry appears in the coverage.

The story reached readers mainly through a Cincinnati dispatch dated January 31, which said the news had "just been received" from Logansport; the Sacramento Daily Record-Union ran a near-identical item under a Logansport dateline. On February 1 it appeared in the Memphis Daily Appeal, the Washington Evening Critic, both Wheeling dailies, the Dallas Daily Herald and the New-York Tribune, among others. The Daily Los Angeles Herald, the Wilmington Daily Gazette and Daily Republican, and the St. Paul Daily Globe carried it the same week. Weekly papers in Wisconsin, Pennsylvania, Ohio, Dakota and Michigan reprinted shorter versions through mid-February, some in news-brief columns between railroad accidents and court items.

Headlines framed the lynching as earned punishment. The Wheeling Register and the Dallas Daily Herald used "Served Him Right," the Wheeling Daily Intelligencer "A Deserved Death," the Los Angeles Herald "Got His Deserts," the Sacramento paper "Diabolical Outrage Promptly Avenaged," and the Evening Critic "Swift Vengeance on an Outrager." Others were plainer, such as the Memphis Daily Appeal's "Rapist Hanged and Burned" and the Millheim Journal's "A Tramp Lynched and Then Burned," but all stated the accusation as fact. The Highland Weekly News called Steele a "miscreant" and said he was hanged "with very little ceremony." No Black-press account from this period is available for comparison.

Versions differ on minor points, all from rewrites of the same dispatch. The Dallas Daily Herald placed the event near "Logansport, Iowa" and gave the woman's name as "Mrs. Buellfordery," while every other version says Indiana and Mrs. Buell. Only the Eaton Democrat gave a direction, "twelve miles south of Logansport."

framing.detail: Headlines 'Served Him Right', 'A Deserved Death', 'Got His Deserts', 'Diabolical Outrage Promptly Avenaged' and 'Swift Vengeance on an Outrager' presented the lynching as deserved punishment.
Most papers ran the Cincinnati wire nearly verbatim under labels such as 'Rapist Hanged and Burned' and 'A Tramp Lynched and Then Burned', stating the accusation as fact.
The Highland Weekly News called Steele a 'villian' and 'miscreant' and described the hanging as done 'with very little ceremony'.
